title: Did Ancient Humans Prefer Hunting Female Mammoths?
gist: A Current Biology study implicates human hunting — rather than natural disaster followed by scavenging — as the source of massive woolly mammoth bone accumulations, resolving a long-standing ambiguity. The captured text lays out the evidence for Paleolithic mammoth harvest and notes that mammoth remains skew male, but stops before answering its own headline question about female mammoths.

insights.claim: Multiple independent lines of evidence point to Late Paleolithic human harvest of mammoths: stone projectile points embedded in bone, cut marks and fractures on mammoth bones found near human settlements, and human bone isotopes showing mammoth meat in Paleolithic diets.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Converging independent proxies — mechanical, contextual, and biochemical — is the evidentiary standard that turns a plausible story into a settled one.
insights.locator: Multiple lines of evidence point to Late Paleolithic

insights.claim: A study published in Current Biology implicates humans as the cause of the massive mammoth bone accumulations found at various sites, which scientists had long debated might instead reflect natural disasters followed by scavenging.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shifts megafauna bone beds from ambiguous taphonomy to direct evidence of human predation pressure — the core of the overkill-hypothesis debate.
insights.locator: Today, a study published in Current Biology

themes.theme: Sex segregation and the male-skewed record

insights.claim: Woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) roamed in sex-segregated herds across the steppe grasslands that once stretched through North America and Eurasia.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Sex-segregated social structure is the mechanism that makes the male/female composition of bone beds informative about how the animals died.

insights.claim: Earlier research interpreted the prevalence of male over female mammoth remains as a product of risky male behavior — falling through thin ice or drowning in pools — rather than as a signature of selective hunting.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: The same skewed dataset supports two rival causal stories; which one wins determines whether humans get blamed for megafauna decline.
insights.locator: The prevalence of male rather than female mammoth remains
